questions.question: In an n=2^k multiplicative subgroup D={1,w,w^2,...,w^{n-1}}, why is -x always in D when x is in D?
options: Because -1 equals w^{n/2}, so -x = (-1)·x stays in the subgroup
Because w is a primitive root of the whole field, so negatives are always powers of w
Because the field prime p is always of the form 2^k+1, so negatives are included
Because D is an additive subgroup, so it is closed under negation
questions.explanation: For even n, w^{n/2} = -1 in the subgroup, so multiplying by -1 maps D to itself.

questions.question: For a non-constant polynomial f(X), what happens to the degree when you form q(X) = (f(X) - f(z)) / (X - z)?
options: It decreases by 1
It stays the same
It increases by 1
It becomes unrelated to deg(f) because of division
questions.explanation: f(X)-f(z) has a root at X=z, so it is divisible by (X-z) and the quotient has degree deg(f)-1.

questions.question: In DEEP quotienting, which identity lets a verifier check that q(x) is consistent with f(x) at a sampled domain point x?
options: f(x) = q(x)·(x - z) + f(z)
q(x) = f(x)·(x - z) + f(z)
f(z) = q(x)·(x - z) + f(x)
questions.explanation: Rearranging q(x)=(f(x)-f(z))/(x-z) gives f(x)=q(x)(x-z)+f(z), checkable pointwise.

questions.question: Which folding formula matches the 2-fold FRI step used in this lesson (for y = x^2)?
options: q_next(y) = (q(x)+q(-x))/2 + beta·(q(x)-q(-x))/(2x)
q_next(y) = (q(x)-q(-x))/2 + beta·(q(x)+q(-x))/(2x)
q_next(y) = q(x^2) + beta·q(-x^2)
q_next(y) = beta·q(x) + (1-beta)·q(-x)
questions.explanation: FRI folding uses even/odd decomposition: g=(q(x)+q(-x))/2 and h=(q(x)-q(-x))/(2x), then q_next=g+beta·h.

questions.question: What does a Merkle 'opening' for one entry in a committed layer consist of?
options: The entry value and a list of sibling hashes proving inclusion up to the root
Only the layer's Merkle root, since the root commits to everything
The entire layer vector, so the verifier can recompute the root
A signature over the value, independent of the Merkle tree
questions.explanation: An opening is the value plus an authentication path (sibling hashes + order) that recomputes the committed root.

questions.question: Why must f(z) (the out-of-domain value) be bound to the transcript (e.g., via Fiat–Shamir) in a non-interactive DEEP-FRI proof?
options: Otherwise the prover can adapt f(z) after seeing queries and keep the quotient checks consistent
Otherwise the field arithmetic becomes invalid and division by (x-z) is undefined
Otherwise Merkle trees stop being collision resistant
Otherwise the verifier cannot compute x^2 during folding
questions.explanation: If f(z) is not fixed before queries, the prover can choose it to satisfy checks at the queried points without representing a single polynomial.

questions.question: Intuitively, what does sampling a random z outside the evaluation domain help prevent?
options: Pretender tables that behave 'low-degree on the grid' but don't match any low-degree polynomial globally
Merkle root collisions caused by internal node hashing
The need for random challenges beta during folding
The verifier having to read more than one layer
questions.explanation: Out-of-domain sampling forces consistency at a random point off the grid, which rules out many structured cheating strategies.

questions.question: In the fold step, why does the formula include division by x (i.e., (q(x)-q(-x))/(2x))?
options: It extracts the 'odd part' h(y) when writing q(x)=g(x^2)+x·h(x^2)
It makes the folded value depend on fewer hash bits
It cancels the Merkle proof path length
It is only needed when p is not prime
questions.explanation: Given q(x)=g(y)+x·h(y) with y=x^2, the difference q(x)-q(-x)=2x·h(y), so dividing by 2x recovers h(y).
